title: Family Zoo — a Chord tutorial
meta: Sixteen steps through the Sharpee engine
subtitle: Sixteen steps through the Sharpee engine
description: Family Zoo — a sixteen-step tutorial for Chord, the Sharpee authoring language, from a single room to a full story.
introHtml:
Family Zoo is a tutorial for Chord, the authoring language of the Sharpee interactive fiction engine. It builds one game across sixteen steps: v01 is a single room in about fifty lines, v16 is the whole zoo in eight hundred — animals with their own verbs, a zookeeper, timed events, scoring, and an after-hours phase.

Every step is a single .story file that is the step before it plus one idea, and every step is playable on its own with its source and test report beside it. Start at v01 to follow it in order, or jump in anywhere.

familyzoo.summary: The finished zoo: eight rooms, animals with their own verbs, a zookeeper, timed events, scoring, and an after-hours phase where the parrot stops being polite. This is every step above, in one 800-line Chord file.
features: `on every turn` — the daemon
`define sequence feeding time` — scripted beats in order
Gating a daemon on a condition so it is not always talking
Keeping ambient text from drowning the player's own actions
`use scoring` in the story header
`score visit worth 5` on a room

familyzoo-v16.summary: The zoo closes. A story state flips, the zookeeper leaves, and the parrot starts speaking candidly — and the parrot's flavour line comes from TypeScript, the one escape hatch Chord keeps.
features: `states: open, after-hours` in the header
`while after-hours` on clauses and descriptions
`define sequence closing time` driving the transition
`define text flavor from "./chord-extras.ts"` (ADR-259)
When to reach for the hatch — and when not to

familyzoo-v15.summary: Points for seeing the zoo. `use scoring` turns on the SCORE command, rooms carry what a visit is worth, and `award` banks it once.
features: `use scoring` in the story header
`score visit worth 5` on a room
`award visit` inside `after the player entering`
Why awarding is idempotent — revisiting pays nothing
The SCORE command, for free

familyzoo-v14.summary: The zoo starts moving on its own: PA announcements, feeding time, goats that get hungrier. A daemon runs every turn; a sequence is a scripted run of beats.
features: `on every turn` — the daemon
`define sequence feeding time` — scripted beats in order
Gating a daemon on a condition so it is not always talking
Keeping ambient text from drowning the player's own actions

familyzoo-v13.summary: Goats, rabbits and the verbs that go with them. In Chord a trait and the action that dispatches on it are one lesson: the trait names a capability, the action is what makes it mean something.
features: `define trait pettable` — naming a capability the stdlib lacks
`define action petting` — a new verb and its grammar
An action that finds its target by trait, not by name
`feedable`, `chatty`, `restless` and animals that carry several traits
Why a trait alone does nothing until an action consults it

familyzoo-v12.summary: The snake, and the three places a story can interrupt the engine: before an action, after it, and on it. This is Chord's answer to event handlers.
features: `on the player <verb>ing` — replace the standard response
`before` — refuse or redirect an action
`after the player entering` — react to arrival
Where a clause belongs: on the thing, not in a central handler

familyzoo-v11.summary: Sam the zookeeper. A person is created like anything else, but carries conversation and reacts to the player being in the room.
features: `a person` and where they stand
`on the player talking to` for conversation
Describing someone doing something, not just standing there
Why the room description mentions them separately

familyzoo-v10.summary: A radio in the supply room, a feed dispenser in the petting zoo, a penny press in the gift shop — and the shop itself, whose description is stitched from a cycling phrase.
features: `switchable` and TURN ON / TURN OFF
`on` clauses that fire when a device is used
`define phrase pins, cycling` — a different line each time
`{pins}` — binding a phrase into a description

familyzoo-v09.summary: A plaque in the aviary. READ is its own action, distinct from EXAMINE, and a phrase block lets the text be laid out the way a sign really reads.
features: `readable` alongside `scenery`
`on the player reading` versus the plain description
A `phrase` block holding multi-paragraph sign text
Why READ and EXAMINE should say different things

familyzoo-v08.summary: The nocturnal exhibit is unlit. Without a light source the player sees nothing; with the flashlight the room opens up. One word on the room does the whole job.
features: `a room, dark`
A portable light source and what carrying it changes
What the engine says when there is no light
A warning sign that tells the player what they need

familyzoo-v07.summary: A staff gate the player cannot pass until they find the keycard. The refusal message is a named phrase in the en-US catalog, not hardcoded English in the exit.
features: `lockable with the staff keycard`
`south is blocked while the staff gate is closed: staff-gate-blocked`
`define phrases en-US` — the catalog of refusal keys
UNLOCK, LOCK and the messages the stdlib already knows

familyzoo-v06.summary: The supply room, its metal shelves and a cork board. `openable` gives a thing an open and a closed state, and OPEN and CLOSE start working with no code of your own.
features: `openable` and the state it implies
A container that is also openable
Rooms reached only through something you must open
Descriptions that read correctly whether open or closed

familyzoo-v05.summary: A backpack that holds things and a park bench that things sit on. Chord distinguishes what is *in* a thing from what is *on* it, and the parser follows.
features: `a container` — things go in it
`a supporter` — things go on it
Putting a thing inside another at creation time
How the room description reports contents it did not have to be told about

familyzoo-v04.summary: The first things the player can carry: a brochure, a map, a souvenir penny. Also the first phrase block — the brochure's text is set verbatim so its layout survives.
features: A thing with no `scenery` is takeable by default
`readable` and `on the player reading`
`define phrase brochure-text, verbatim` — text kept exactly as written
TAKE, DROP and INVENTORY come from the standard library

familyzoo-v03.summary: Fences, flower beds, hay, a waterfall, a toucan. Scenery is what makes a room feel like a place rather than a list of exits — present to examine, refused when taken.
features: `scenery` blocks taking without any refusal message of your own
Several scenery things sharing one room
Writing descriptions that reward a second look
`aka` on scenery so EXAMINE FENCE and EXAMINE IRON FENCE both work

familyzoo-v02.summary: The zoo grows to four rooms joined by compass directions. Exits are one line each, and `aka` gives every room the names a player will actually type.
features: `south to the Main Path` — an exit is a property of the room
Exits are declared one way; Chord wires the return trip
`aka path, gravel path` for synonyms the parser accepts
Room descriptions that tell the player where the exits go

familyzoo-v01.summary: The smallest Chord story that runs: a header that names the work, one room, and two pieces of scenery you can examine. Everything else in the tutorial is added to this.
features: The `story` header — `title`, `authors`, `id`, `description`
`create the <Room>` with `a room` and an indented description
`scenery` for things that belong to the room and cannot be taken
`in the <Room>` to place a thing
`before the game starts` naming who the player is
